items.content:
The owner had already changed the battery once.

A few days later, the same thing happened again.

The car would sit overnight and by morning the battery was weak enough that starting it became a problem. At first, everything pointed toward the usual suspects: alternator, interior lights, an accessory staying powered, or maybe just another bad battery.

But when I started looking at the vehicle network, something else stood out.

The ignition was off, the doors were closed, and the car had been sitting long enough that most of the control modules should have started going to sleep.

The CAN bus was still busy.

That caught my attention.

Modern cars do not shut everything down immediately after you turn the ignition off. Some modules stay awake for a while to save data, monitor the alarm system, manage locks, communicate with other ECUs, and finish background tasks.

But after a certain period, most of that activity should reduce significantly.

So I connected to the CAN interface and watched the traffic.

At first, there were plenty of frames moving across the bus, which was normal.

Then the traffic slowly started dropping as different modules went quiet.

Except for one group of CAN IDs.

They kept appearing.

Minute after minute.

I checked the bus activity again and it was still higher than I expected for a vehicle that should have been settling into its sleep state.

That gave me something real to investigate.

One module, or something connected to it, appeared to be keeping part of the network awake.

And when one ECU refuses to sleep, it can sometimes keep other modules awake with it. That means several electronic systems can continue drawing power for hours while the car is parked.

From the owner’s perspective, it looks like a battery problem.

From the network side, it looks completely different.

Now, this does not automatically mean anything malicious is happening.

A bad body control module, faulty door sensor, infotainment system, telematics unit, wiring issue, software bug, or another ECU can all cause similar behaviour.

But instead of replacing another battery and hoping for the best, the CAN traffic gives you somewhere to start.

Which module is still transmitting?

When should it normally stop?

Is something waking the network back up?

Does the same CAN ID remain active every time the vehicle is switched off?

This is one reason I find automobile cybersecurity auditing so interesting.

Sometimes the problem people see as purely mechanical or electrical is actually sitting quietly inside the communication between the computers running the car.

FalconForceのOlaf Hartong氏は、Windowsのテレメトリ基盤ETW(Event Tracing for Windows)を悪用し、管理者権限なしの一般ユーザーコンテキストからMicrosoft Defender for Endpoint(MDE)へ偽イベントを注入できることを実証した。多くのプロバイダーは登録に強い権限を要求しないため、正規プロバイダーと同一GUIDで別プロセスが偽装登録し、マニフェスト形式を正確に模倣したイベントを送信すれば、MDEのクラウド側にも偽のLDAP検索イベントなどが到達してしまう。

さらに深刻なのはバッファプールの仕組みである。ETWのリアルタイムセッションはセッション単位でバッファを共有しており、消費側が排出を怠りプールが満杯になると、そのセッションに接続する全プロバイダーが新規イベント発行を停止させられる。これにより攻撃者が意図的にバッファを溢れさせるだけで、EDRのETW由来の可視性を完全に失わせる「盲目化」が可能になる。加えてクラウドEDR特有のイベント上限(キャッピング)機構を悪用し、無害なノイズで上限を先に消費させてから本命の攻撃を実行すれば、そのテレメトリはクラウドに届かない。マルウェア検知や身代金要求型攻撃を模した偽アラートを大量発生させ、アナリストの注意を逸らす手口も実演された。

RT @BabyD1111229: A police chief in Oshkosh, Wisconsin caught Flock lying to his city council, and killed the $8 billion surveillance company's contract less than a day after the council had approved it.

Here's how it happened.

The night before, Oshkosh's council was set to renew its deal with Flock Safety, the license plate camera company backed by a16z and Tiger Global.

One council member asked the Flock rep a plain yes-or-no question. Does this system build a heat map of everywhere a specific car travels over time?

Flock's rep said no.

The council believed him and voted 5 to 2 to renew. By the next morning, Chief Dean Smith's own officers had told him that answer was false.

So he pulled up the system himself. He watched it generate the exact heat map Flock had just sworn it couldn't make.

Then he walked into an emergency meeting and said it out loud: "Because of this misrepresentation, I can no longer recommend Flock."

Understand what a heat map is, because it's the whole trick.

Flock sells cities a tidy little story. A car drives by, we snap a photo, we read the plate, that's all it is.

But the same system can quietly average out where your car goes day after day and paint your routine onto a map.

Not one snapshot at one corner. Your pattern. Where you sleep, where you work, where you keep going back and how often.

A Flock employee later admitted on the record that the software does exactly that.
So the pitch and the product are two different things. The company wins the contract selling a plate reader, then sits on a moving map of your life.

The only reason Oshkosh caught it was one skeptical question and a police chief who bothered to check the answer.

The vote to rescind was 7 to 0. Unanimous.

Flock called the whole thing "one small misconception" from a long meeting and said it was disappointed nobody let it explain.

A surveillance company worth eight billion dollars got caught lying about whether it maps where you drive. Its defense was that the lie was small.

Oshkosh got one honest answer by accident. Congress can make it the rule.
